title: No, Sir; We Have No Such Intention: the One Question Parliament Asked After November 1890
participants: Mr Goschen, Chancellor of the Exchequer

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: Not documented here, and this dossier invents nothing. The record read contains no figure of any kind — no exposure, no guarantee, no loss, no name of any firm.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What the record gives is the standing structural complaint, in a Member's own words: "the continual annual strain put upon business by the decrease in the Bank reserve, and constant scarcity of gold", under an Act of 1844 that a Member thought no longer "in keeping with the present time, and the expansion of business which has taken place since the Act was passed".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is in the naming. The only parliamentary reference found to the episode calls it "the recent serious crisis in the City". The failed house is never identified; neither "Baring" nor "Argentine" appears anywhere in the debate. A rescue large enough to require the Bank of England's organisation reached the floor of the Commons once, as an adjective.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Not documented in what was read. Who was guaranteed, by whom, on what terms, and who gained, is absent from the record examined, and no claim about it is made here.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: This is the whole of what the record delivers, and it delivers it cleanly. Asked whether the Government would appoint a Royal Commission "to inquire into the whole question of the working of the Bank Act of 1844", Mr Goschen answered: "No, Sir; we have no such intention. If at any time it should appear to Her Majesty's Government that the arrangements made in 1844 should be altered in any particulars, they would prefer to deal with the matter on their own initiative and responsibility rather than to relegate the matter to a Royal Commission." Asked the same sitting about amending the Act, he said he was "not prepared at the present moment to make any declaration of policy as regards the Bank Charter Act". Within days of Parliament reconvening after the rescue, an inquiry was refused and a policy statement declined.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Bank Charter Act 1844 and the reserve arrangements it fixed — the same statute whose suspension by Treasury letter the Commons had debated in 1847, 1857 and 1866.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: Nothing, which is the finding. The Government declined both an amending Bill and a Royal Commission, and stated a preference for acting "on their own initiative and responsibility" if it ever moved at all.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Not traced by this source. The loop this dossier can show is procedural rather than financial: a crisis passes, the legislature asks whether the governing statute should be examined, the executive says it would rather decide alone, and the arrangement survives unexamined into the next crisis.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Bank of England secretly bailed out Baring Brothers in November 1890 with a guarantee fund organised to spare the City's most connected house, and that the whole thing was buried.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: IT IS NOT THAT THE DECOY FAILS HERE; IT IS THAT THIS RECORD CANNOT TEST IT, AND THE DOSSIER SAYS SO INSTEAD OF IMPLYING OTHERWISE. What was read is the official record of Parliament, searched across the November and December 1890 and January and February 1891 sittings by debate title for "Baring", "Argentine", "Bank of England", "Bank Act", "gold reserve", "money market" and "financial". The search produced exactly one debate about the episode, and in it the episode is unnamed: "the recent serious crisis in the City". No figure, no firm, no guarantee and no beneficiary appears. The Bank of England's own records of November 1890 were not read, and this dossier makes no claim about what the rescue consisted of or who benefited from it. What the single debate does establish is the one thing a legislature's record is best at establishing: what was asked, and what was refused. A Member asked for a short Bill to amend the Bank Act of 1844; the Chancellor would make no declaration of policy. Another asked for a Royal Commission on the working of that Act; the answer was "No, Sir; we have no such intention", with a stated preference for the Government dealing with it "on their own initiative and responsibility". An inquiry into the statute that had just been tested was declined within the first week the House sat. THE HONEST SUMMARY OF THIS NODE: it is thin, and it is thin because the record is. One question, one refusal, and a crisis that Parliament did not name.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A single exchange in the House of Commons on 27 November 1890, printed in Hansard at vol 349 c125. Mr Ernest Spencer asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether, "in view of the recent serious crisis in the City, and the continual annual strain put upon business by the decrease in the Bank reserve, and constant scarcity of gold", the Government would consider a short Bill to amend the Bank Act of 1844 by issuing £1 notes against silver or Consols. Mr Goschen replied that he was "not prepared at the present moment to make any declaration of policy as regards the Bank Charter Act", nor to admit the second part of the question as a necessary corollary to the first. Mr Lea then asked whether the Government intended to appoint a Royal Commission to inquire into the whole question of the working of the Bank Act of 1844, and when. Mr Goschen replied: "No, Sir; we have no such intention. If at any time it should appear to Her Majesty's Government that the arrangements made in 1844 should be altered in any particulars, they would prefer to deal with the matter on their own initiative and responsibility rather than to relegate the matter to a Royal Commission." This is the only debate heading on the crisis found across the sittings of November and December 1890 and January and February 1891, and it does not name the firm that failed.

citations.title: House of Commons, "THE BANK ACT—£1 NOTES.", HC Deb 27 November 1890 vol 349 c125 (Historic Hansard)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on Parliament's own Historic Hansard service; the entire exchange is quoted below, because it is short and because its brevity is the point. MR. ERNEST SPENCER (West Bromwich): "I beg to ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether, in view of the recent serious crisis in the City, and the continual annual strain put upon business by the decrease in the Bank reserve, and constant scarcity of gold, the Government will now consider the advisability of introducing a short Bill to amend the Bank Act of 1844 by the issue of £1 notes against silver, or Consols, or otherwise, in order that it may be in keeping with the present time, and the expansion of business which has taken place since the Act was passed?" MR. GOSCHEN: "I am not prepared at the present moment to make any declaration of policy as regards the Bank Charter Act, nor am I prepared to admit the second part of my hon. Friend's question as a necessary corollary to the first." MR. LEA (Londonderry, S.): "I have also to ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer if the Government intend to appoint a Royal Commission to inquire into the whole question of the working of the Bank Act of 1844; if so, when such Royal Commission will be appointed?" MR. GOSCHEN: "No, Sir; we have no such intention. If at any time it should appear to Her Majesty's Government that the arrangements made in 1844 should be altered in any particulars, they would prefer to deal with the matter on their own initiative and responsibility rather than to relegate the matter to a Royal Commission." WHAT THIS IS AND WHAT IT IS NOT. It is the Chancellor of the Exchequer, in the first week Parliament sat after the November 1890 rescue, refusing an inquiry into the statute governing the Bank of England's reserve, and stating a preference for acting "on their own initiative and responsibility" instead. It is also the only occasion found, across the whole of the November and December 1890 and the January and February 1891 sittings, on which the episode reaches the floor at all: the sitting indexes for those months were searched by title for "Baring", "Argentine", "Bank of England", "Bank Act", "gold reserve", "money market" and "financial", and this is the only debate heading about the crisis. THE FIRM IS NEVER NAMED. Mr Spencer says only "the recent serious crisis in the City"; neither "Baring" nor "Argentine" appears. Nothing here describes the rescue, its terms, who guaranteed what, or who gained or lost by it, and no such claim is made from this source. The Bank of England's own records of November 1890 were not read.
